analysis.one_liner: Requires every person in the U.S. aged 18 to 42 to perform two years of national service, military or civilian.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it attracted zero cosponsors and sat in a House subcommittee until the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make national service a legal obligation for every U.S. citizen and every other person living in the country between ages 18 and 42. Each person would owe two years of service, either in uniform or in a civilian job the President decides promotes national defense, including community and homeland security work. People could be forced into military service only during a declared war, a declared national emergency, or an authorized combat operation; everyone else would serve in a civilian capacity. The President would write the rules on who serves where, who is deferred or exempted, and what happens to those who don't perform their service.
analysis.who_benefits: The armed forces would gain a standing pool of inductees whenever the country is at war or in a declared emergency, ending reliance on volunteers alone. Civilian service programs in national defense, homeland security, and community service would gain a guaranteed workforce. Supporters of the idea argue the public also gains because the burden of fighting wars would be shared by everyone rather than falling on volunteers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The armed forces and civilian service programs

how_it_helps.text: Gives the President authority to induct people into uniformed service when a declaration of war is in effect, during a national emergency the President declares, or when troops are engaged in an authorized contingency operation, with random selection for who is called [S3].
Assigns everyone not inducted into the military to a two-year civilian service obligation promoting national defense, homeland security, or community service [S2] [S3].
Protects conscientious objectors from combatant training and service, allowing them to serve in noncombatant or civilian roles instead [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Every person aged 18 to 42 living in the United States, including non-citizens, would owe two years of their life to mandatory service, with deferments only for high school students, extreme hardship, or disability. People in that age range would put schooling, careers, and family plans on hold; employers would lose workers for two years; and anyone deemed to have failed their civilian service would face penalties set by presidential regulation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone aged 18 to 42 and their employers

drawbacks.text: It would compel two years of labor from every person aged 18 to 42 residing in the U.S., including non-citizens, disrupting education, careers, and families on a mass scale [S3].

The President would decide what counts as civilian service, what standards people must meet, and the penalties for failing to perform satisfactorily, giving the executive sweeping discretion over compelled work [S3].

Deferments for hardship or disability would end as soon as their cause ends, and the only bright-line protections are for current high school students and those already serving or in service academies, leaving most people with no way out [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill rests on fairness: during a war, everyone shares the burden instead of volunteers and their families carrying it. The cost is enormous and one-sided — a legally compelled two-year obligation for tens of millions of people, with detailed rules left to presidential regulation. The idea drew no cosponsors from either party, and no committee in Congress treated it as a serious proposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2010 with no cosponsors, referred to the House Armed Services Committee and then to its Military Personnel Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2011 without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Rangel introduced the Universal National Service Act in the House on July 15, 2010 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services on the day of introduction and to the Subcommittee on Military Personnel a week later [S5].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill received no further action and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People aged 18 to 42 came out ahead: no one was ever subject to a mandatory two-year service obligation, and the armed forces continued to rely on volunteers as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Adults under 42 who owed no service

for.name: Rep. Charles B. Rangel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; no one else signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Armed Services
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Military Personnel Subcommittee and never brought it back for consideration, a markup, or a vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Military Personnel
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 23, 2010 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no party split — just a single sponsor and zero support.

industries.note: The military would gain a compelled pool of inductees during wars, national emergencies, and authorized combat operations, ending full reliance on volunteers. The gain comes directly at the cost of two years of compelled service from ordinary adults.

Civilian service programs in homeland security and community service would receive a guaranteed two-year workforce. The public would benefit from the work done but pay for it through a legal obligation on every young adult.
Businesses employing people in the covered age range would lose those workers for two years, though some might eventually employ discharged service members afterward.
